metadata.title: Motivation towards mathematics from 1980 to 2015: Exploring the feasibility of trend scaling

survey_design.weight_variable_name: senate weights (rescaled stratum weights in SIMS; rescaled within-country for grade equalization in TIMSS 1995)
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pooled grade 8 (or equivalent) student questionnaire data across seven ILSA cycles: SIMS 1980 and TIMSS 1995–2015, using only five educational systems that participated in all time points (England, Hong Kong, Hungary, Israel, Japan, United States). To address unequal country sample sizes and the TIMSS 1995 design where two adjacent grades were sampled in most countries (except Israel), the authors applied senate weights that sum to 500 for each country’s data. In SIMS, stratum weights were rescaled to senate weights, and in TIMSS 1995 the senate weights were further rescaled so that each grade contributed equally within a country. These weights were used in the scaling procedures (CFA/IRT/market-basket) to ensure each country contributed equally to the estimation of the motivation scales and their trend components.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables in this study are affective motivation constructs (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) derived from questionnaire items and then scaled via CFA/IRT/market-basket procedures, rather than cognitive achievement outcomes for which PVs are typically generated in ILSA. Missing data handling is reported via model-based approaches in Mplus (FIML/MLR with robust SEs) and via the market-basket procedure that generates plausible responses for missing-by-design items, which corresponds to multiple imputation of item responses (five imputations per respondent).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset was constructed by pooling grade 8 (or equivalent) student questionnaire data from seven ILSA mathematics motivation administrations: SIMS 1980 and TIMSS 1995, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011, and 2015. The authors restricted the pooled analysis to six educational systems that participated in all time points: England, Hong Kong, Hungary, Israel, Japan, and the United States. For the cross-cultural latent-variable analyses (MGCFA and subsequent latent-variable scaling), Japan was excluded after failing measurement invariance in the baseline MGCFA at each time point (negative factor loadings for multiple items). For the market-basket scaling, the study treated countries as separate measurement models to generate plausible responses for items not included in each cycle, and it did not treat the SIMS “middle/undecided” response option as missing; instead, middle responses were recoded to random answers between agree/disagree, with students selecting the middle option for all items excluded (0.95% for extrinsic and 0.71% for intrinsic).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged Motivation scale type, Country (educational system), Assessment year (time point) to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study investigates whether two affective mathematics motivation constructs—extrinsic and intrinsic motivation—can be placed on a comparable trend scale from 1980 to 2015 using questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS 1995–2015. The authors pooled grade 8 (or equivalent) responses for six educational systems (England, Hong Kong, Hungary, Israel, Japan, United States) and assessed cross-cultural measurement equivalence using MGCFA (categorical items, WLSMV estimator) and longitudinal item parameter drift using Angoff’s delta plot method. For scaling, they compared three approaches: CFA-based scaling, IRT-based scaling (PCM vs GPCM, with GPCM selected), and a market-basket approach that generates plausible responses for missing-by-design items using country-specific measurement models. They report that individual-level correlations across scaling methods were very high (0.96 to 1), and country-level trends from CFA/IRT under invariance assumptions closely matched observed scores. A key limitation is that standard errors of country means may be underestimated because the TIMSS stratified multistage sampling design violates the simple random sampling assumption used for standard error calculations. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This study investigates whether two affective mathematics motivation constructs—extrinsic and intrinsic motivation—can be placed on a comparable trend scale from 1980 to 2015 using questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS 1995–2015. For scaling, they compared three approaches: CFA-based scaling, IRT-based scaling (PCM vs GPCM, with GPCM selected), and a market-basket approach that generates plausible responses for missing-by-design items using country-specific measurement models. They report that individual-level correlations across scaling methods were very high (0.96 to 1), and country-level trends from CFA/IRT under invariance assumptions closely matched observed scores. data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction study: it focuses on measurement invariance, item drift, and constructing comparable trend scales for affective motivation using CFA/IRT and a market-basket plausible-response approach. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, no predictive target variable, and no model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE/AUC) to extract into main_findings. The absence of main_findings rows reflects the study’s psychometric/scaling objective rather than supervised ML evaluation.
